fields.explanation: The threshold sentence occurs in the contraposition branch (operation neither projection nor constant), not under the original all-congruences premise. The exact three-point witness executes the next equivalence-relation step. S={a,b,c}; cc=b, all other products=a. All three operation exclusions and printed inequalities hold. Classes{a,c},{b} distinguish products. Actual Fin3 cardinality and Setoid, with the original operation; all relations and inequalities are kernel checked.
fields.flaw: The proof asserts that the configuration it just described (elements x1,y1,x2,y2 with z1 = x1∘y1, z2 = x2∘y2, z1 ≠ z2, ¬(z1=x1 ∧ z2=x2), ¬(z1=y1 ∧ z2=y2), for an operation ∘ that is none of the right/left/constant operations) can occur only when |S| > 3. This is false: an explicit 3-element set with an explicit operation table realizes all of the stated conditions, so the proof's cardinality claim (which would also wrongly exclude the |S| = 3 case allowed by the hypothesis "at least 3 elements") is refuted by a finite witness.
fields.problem:
Title: Operation on Set for which Every Equivalence Relation is Congruence

Let $S$ be a [[Definition:Set|set]] with at least $3$ [[Definition:Element|elements]].

Let $\circ$ be an [[Definition:Binary Operation|operation]] on $S$ such that every [[Definition:Equivalence Relation|equivalence relation]] on $S$ is a [[Definition:Congruence Relation|congruence relation]] for $\circ$.

Then $\circ$ is one of the following:
:the [[Definition:Right Operation|right operation]] $\to$
:the [[Definition:Left Operation|left operation]] $\gets$
:the [[Definition:Constant Operation|constant operation]] $\sqbrk c$ for some $c \in S$.
fields.source_context:
0008 | Let $\circ$ be an [[Definition:Binary Operation|operation]] on $S$ which is ''not'' one of those three.
0009 | 
0010 | Then there exists $x_1, x_2, y_1, y_2 \in S$ such that:
0011 | :$x_1 \circ y_1 = z_1$
0012 | :$x_2 \circ y_2 = z_2$
0013 | 
0014 | where:
0015 | 
0016 | :$z_1 \ne z_2$
0017 | :$\map \lnot {z_1 = x_1 \land z_2 = x_2}$
0018 | :$\map \lnot {z_1 = y_1 \land z_2 = y_2}$
0019 | 
0020 | The above are possible only if there are more than $3$ [[Definition:Element|elements]] in $S$.
0021 | 
0022 | Let $\RR$ be an [[Definition:Equivalence Relation|equivalence relation]] on $S$ such that:
0023 | 
0024 | :$x_1 \mathrel \RR x_2$
0025 | :$y_1 \mathrel \RR y_2$
0026 | 
0027 | but that:
0028 | :$\map \lnot {z_1 \mathrel \RR z_2}$
0029 | 
0030 | Then $\RR$ is not a [[Definition:Congruence Relation|congruence relation]].
0031 | 
0032 | The result follows from the [[Rule of Transposition]].
fields.witness: Use S = {a,b,c}. Define c o c = b and every other product to be a. Take (x1,y1)=(a,a), so z1=a, and (x2,y2)=(c,c), so z2=b. The operation is neither left projection, right projection, nor constant; z1 != z2; and both printed negated-conjunction conditions hold. Moreover, the equivalence relation generated by x1~x2 and y1~y2 has classes {a,c} and {b}, so it separates z1 from z2 and the proof's next step is executable. All conditions therefore occur on exactly three elements, contradicting the printed requirement |S|>3.
